scenes.title: Foundation: rank, transpose and inverse
scenes.objective: Recall the matrix facts needed for generalized inverses.

ask.q: When does an ordinary inverse A⁻¹ exist?
ask.nudge: A must be square and nonsingular.

body: The ordinary inverse is defined only for a square full-rank matrix. Statistical design matrices are often rectangular or rank deficient, so an ordinary inverse may not exist.
A generalized inverse extends useful inverse identities to arbitrary matrices. It supports least-squares solutions, projection matrices and estimability in linear models.

items.recall: The dimension of the column space, equal to the dimension of the row space.
refresh: Rank counts the independent directions carried by a matrix. A matrix of order m×n has rank at most min(m,n).
Full column rank means all columns are independent; full row rank means all rows are independent. These two cases have different simple Moore–Penrose formulas.

items.recall: The set of x satisfying Ax=0.
refresh: The null space contains coefficient directions that the matrix sends to zero. Its dimension is n−rank(A) for an m×n matrix.
In a linear model, a non-zero null-space direction represents a change in coefficients that leaves fitted values unchanged. This is why rank deficiency creates non-unique coefficient representations.

items.ask: What is a symmetric idempotent matrix?
items.recall: A matrix P with Pᵀ=P and P²=P.
refresh: Symmetry and idempotence are the defining properties of an orthogonal projection matrix. It projects vectors onto its column space.
The Moore–Penrose inverse creates projection matrices AA⁺ and A⁺A, which are symmetric and idempotent. These matrices are central to least squares and estimability.

scenes.title: Why a generalized inverse is useful
scenes.objective: Understand what the extension makes possible.

ask.q: If X is rectangular or rank deficient, can (XᵀX)⁻¹ always be used?
ask.nudge: Only if X has full column rank.

body: Many statistical matrices are rectangular. Even when X is square, exact linear dependence can make it singular. The ordinary inverse then fails.
A generalized inverse supplies a matrix G satisfying AGA=A. The Moore–Penrose inverse adds symmetry conditions that select one unique generalized inverse for every real matrix.

ask.q: What identity defines a generalized inverse G of A?
ask.nudge: A, G, A in that order.

blocks.body: G is a generalized inverse of A if AGA=A. Such a G exists for every real matrix A.
A reflexive generalized inverse additionally satisfies GAG=G. The two identities are AGA=A and GAG=G.
A generalized inverse need not be unique. The Moore–Penrose inverse adds two symmetry conditions and is unique.

scenes.title: Worked: a simple singular matrix
scenes.objective: Find and verify the Moore–Penrose inverse.

ask.nudge: This matrix is already its own Moore–Penrose inverse.

scenes.problem: Find the Moore–Penrose inverse of A=[[1,0],[0,0]].

steps.say: Check the first two Penrose identities.
Check symmetry of AG and GA.
steps.why: All four Moore–Penrose conditions hold, so G=A⁺.

scenario.teaser: A redundant predictor makes a design matrix rank deficient.
scenario.title: A generalized inverse in an over-specified regression
body: Suppose two columns of a design matrix are identical. The coefficient vector is not uniquely determined: adding a value to one coefficient and subtracting it from the other leaves fitted values unchanged.

The ordinary inverse (XᵀX)⁻¹ does not exist. The Moore–Penrose inverse X⁺ still gives a least-squares solution, selecting the minimum-Euclidean-norm coefficient vector among all least-squares solutions.
The fitted vector XX⁺y is unique even when the coefficient representation is not. This separates prediction from parameter identifiability.

ask.q: Which two products must be symmetric for the Moore–Penrose inverse?
ask.nudge: The products are AA⁺ and A⁺A.

blocks.body: Every real matrix has exactly one Moore–Penrose inverse satisfying all four equations. It is denoted A⁺.
AA⁺ is the orthogonal projection onto Col(A). A⁺A is the orthogonal projection onto Row(A), viewed as a subspace of the domain.

scenes.title: Guided: full column rank formula
scenes.objective: Use the simplified formula when columns are independent.
scenes.problem: Let A be m×n with full column rank. State A⁺.
hints: Full column rank makes AᵀA invertible.
scenes.solution: When A has full column rank, AᵀA is nonsingular. The Moore–Penrose inverse is (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ, and A⁺A=Iₙ.

ask.q: What is A⁺A in this full-column-rank case?

scenes.title: Full row rank and projection matrices

ask.q: If A has full row rank, what is A⁺?

blocks.body: For A of order m×n with rank m, A⁺=Aᵀ(AAᵀ)⁻¹ and AA⁺=Iₘ.
AA⁺ is symmetric and idempotent, projecting onto Col(A). A⁺A is symmetric and idempotent, projecting onto Row(A).
Use the four Penrose equations or an SVD to obtain A⁺. Do not use (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ unless A has full column rank.

scenes.title: Guided: estimability
scenes.objective: Use row-space membership to test a linear function.
scenes.problem: In y=Xβ+ε, when is cᵀβ estimable?
hints: A linear function is estimable if it can be written as a linear combination of the expected observations.
The condition is c=Xᵀa for some vector a.
Equivalently, c belongs to Row(X) and is orthogonal to Null(X).
scenes.answer: cᵀβ is estimable iff c∈Row(X), equivalently c=Xᵀa for some a.
scenes.solution: E(y)=Xβ. A linear combination aᵀE(y)=aᵀXβ=(Xᵀa)ᵀβ. Thus cᵀβ is estimable exactly when c=Xᵀa, which is row-space membership.

ask.q: If X has full column rank, are all linear functions cᵀβ estimable?
ask.nudge: Its row space is the entire parameter space.

scenes.title: Least squares and the projection

ask.nudge: It lies in Col(X) and the residual is orthogonal to Col(X).

body: The Moore–Penrose solution β̂=X⁺y gives fitted values Xβ̂=XX⁺y. The matrix XX⁺ is symmetric and idempotent, so it is the orthogonal projector onto the column space of X.
The residual y−XX⁺y is orthogonal to every column of X. This is the normal-equation condition Xᵀ(y−Xβ̂)=0, and it holds even when the coefficient vector is not unique.

scenario.teaser: The fitted values remain unique despite non-unique coefficients.
scenario.title: Least squares with redundant predictors
body: When columns of X are linearly dependent, several coefficient vectors can produce the same fitted vector. The ordinary normal-equation inverse fails, but least-squares fitted values remain well-defined.
The Moore–Penrose inverse chooses the minimum-norm coefficient solution β̂=X⁺y. The fitted vector XX⁺y is the orthogonal projection of y onto Col(X).
Thus prediction can be unique even when individual regression coefficients are not identifiable. Estimability asks which linear combinations of those coefficients are determined by the model.

scenes.title: Worked: test estimability
scenes.objective: Use a null-space direction to reject a non-estimable contrast.

ask.q: If Null(X) contains (1,−1), is β₁+β₂ estimable?
ask.nudge: The contrast vector (1,1) is not orthogonal to (1,−1)? Check the dot product.

scenes.problem: Suppose Null(X)=span{(1,−1)}. Is cᵀβ estimable for c=(1,1)ᵀ and for d=(1,0)ᵀ?

steps.say: Use orthogonality to the null space.
steps.why: c is orthogonal to the null space, so c lies in Row(X) and is estimable.
d is not orthogonal to the null space, so d is not in Row(X).

steps.math: β₁+β₂ is estimable; β₁ alone is not.
steps.why: Estimability is determined by row-space membership, not by whether a particular generalized inverse returns a coefficient.

scenes.title: Trap check: six statements
scenes.intro: Judge each statement true or false.

items.claim: Every real matrix has a Moore–Penrose inverse.
items.why: The four Penrose equations have a unique solution for every real matrix.

items.claim: A generalized inverse is always unique.
items.why: The condition AGA=A alone does not ensure uniqueness.
The four Penrose equations select exactly one matrix.

items.claim: For full column rank A, A⁺=(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀ.
items.why: AᵀA is invertible in this case.

items.claim: Every coefficient in a rank-deficient model is estimable.
items.why: Only contrasts in Row(X) are estimable.

items.claim: AA⁺ is the orthogonal projector onto Col(A).
items.why: It is symmetric, idempotent and has column space Col(A).

2. Moore–Penrose inverse: all four Penrose equations; unique for every real matrix.

6. Least-squares fitted vector is XX⁺y; residual is orthogonal to Col(X).
